title: INS v. Chadha (1983)
summary: Congress can alter the legal rights, duties and relations of persons outside the legislative branch only by passing a bill through both Houses and presenting it to the President, so the one-House veto of the Attorney General’s suspension of a deportation was unconstitutional; the veto was severable, leaving the suspension power intact.
notes:
Key line: By the same token, the fact that a given law or procedure is efficient, convenient, and useful in facilitating functions of government, standing alone, will not save it if it is contrary to the Constitution. (Chief Justice Burger)

Citation: 462 U.S. 919 (1983).

sections.Parties: Jagdish Rai Chadha, of East Indian origin, born in Kenya and holding a British passport, was the person ordered deported; he petitioned the Ninth Circuit and was an appellee and respondent in the Supreme Court. The Immigration and Naturalization Service, which administered the statute for the Attorney General, was the appellant even though it agreed with Chadha that the legislative veto was unconstitutional, because it would enforce the deportation order unless a court prevented it. The House of Representatives and the Senate defended the veto, intervened, and filed their own petitions for certiorari.
sections.Material Facts: Chadha lawfully entered the United States in 1966 on a student visa that expired on June 30, 1972, and stayed. On October 11, 1973 the INS ordered him to show cause why he should not be deported; he conceded deportability and applied under § 244(a)(1) for suspension of deportation. An immigration judge suspended his deportation on June 25, 1974 and reported it to Congress. Under § 244(c)(2) either House could, before the end of the next session, adopt a resolution disapproving the suspension, in which case the Attorney General had to deport. On December 12, 1975 Representative Eilberg introduced House Resolution 926 opposing permanent residence for six aliens, including Chadha, after his subcommittee reviewed 340 suspensions. On December 16 the House adopted it without printing, debate or a recorded vote; it went neither to the Senate nor to the President. Chadha was ordered deported on November 8, 1976.
sections.Procedural History: The immigration judge and the Board of Immigration Appeals held they had no power to decide whether § 244(c)(2) was constitutional and dismissed Chadha’s appeal. He petitioned the Ninth Circuit for review under § 106(a). The INS agreed the veto was unconstitutional, so the court invited the House and Senate to file briefs as amici. The Ninth Circuit held that the House lacked constitutional authority to order Chadha’s deportation by this mechanism and directed the Attorney General not to deport him on the basis of the resolution, 634 F.2d 408 (1980). The INS appealed under 28 U.S.C. § 1252 and both Houses petitioned for certiorari; the Court heard argument on February 22, 1982 and reargument on December 7, 1982, and affirmed on June 23, 1983. Chief Justice Burger wrote for six Justices; Justice Powell concurred in the judgment; Justice White dissented; Justice Rehnquist, joined by White, dissented on severability.
sections.Issue: May Congress authorize either House, acting alone and without presentment to the President, to overturn the Attorney General’s suspension of an individual’s deportation? Is the House’s action legislative in character, so that Article I requires bicameral passage and presentment, or may it operate as a condition reserved when Congress delegated the suspension authority? If the veto is unconstitutional, is it severable from the suspension power, and do the parties’ alignment and the possibility of other immigration relief prevent decision?
sections.Holding: Yes to jurisdiction and justiciability: the INS was aggrieved by a judgment that barred it from executing an order it would otherwise enforce; Chadha had standing and faced a concrete injury; possible alternative relief was speculative; Congress’s defense supplied adversity; and Congress’s plenary power over immigration did not make the constitutionality of its procedure a political question. On the merits, when Congress takes action that is legislative in purpose and effect it must comply with bicameralism and presentment unless the Constitution itself provides otherwise. The House resolution altered the legal rights, duties and relations of Chadha and executive officials outside the legislative branch, so § 244(c)(2)’s one-House veto was unconstitutional. The provision was severable under the Act’s severability clause, leaving the suspension power and reporting requirement in place. The Ninth Circuit was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: The severability clause created a presumption that Congress did not intend the whole scheme to depend on the veto. On the merits Burger began with Article I, §§ 1 and 7: legislative power is vested in a Congress of two Houses, bills must pass both and be presented to the President, and § 7, clause 3 extends presentment to orders, resolutions and votes so that Congress cannot evade it by renaming its action. The resolution was legislative in character because of what it did: it overruled the Attorney General’s decision and imposed a duty to deport; once Congress delegated the authority it had to respect the delegation until it legislated again. The Attorney General’s own action differed because it was taken under an enacted law and reviewable for conformity to it. The Constitution names four situations in which one House acts alone with binding effect (impeachment, impeachment trial, appointments, treaties), and this was not among them. Nearly two hundred statutes had used legislative vetoes, but efficiency and convenience cannot save a procedure contrary to the Constitution.

topics.lrs-s-congressional-control: A retained congressional veto had to satisfy the constitutionally prescribed process for legislation.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Powell concurred in the judgment on a narrower ground: by deciding that six named individuals failed the statutory hardship criteria, the House assumed a judicial function without the safeguards of a hearing or an impartial tribunal. Justice White dissented, defending the legislative veto as an accommodation between broad delegation and congressional responsibility: agency rules also change legal rights without passing both Houses, and the veto was a condition built into an Article I statute, so a permanent change in Chadha’s status required the functional agreement of the Executive, House and Senate. Justice Rehnquist, joined by White, dissented on severability, because Congress had repeatedly refused to give the Executive unconditional suspension authority.
